scenarios.title: The Monday-morning hire
scenarios.situation: New hires wait 3 days for accounts, groups, and app access — all provisioned by manual tickets.
scenarios.prompt: What automates the joiner process?
evidence: Review the relevant user-group-lifecycle documentation.
choices: Lifecycle workflows + dynamic groups + group-based licensing/app assignment — HR-driven provisioning from day one
More help-desk staff
A shared new-hire account
Emailing IT faster
scenarios.why: Entra lifecycle workflows trigger joiner/mover/leaver tasks (account creation, group adds, access packages, manager notifications) from HR signals. Combined with dynamic groups, day-one access becomes automatic instead of ticket-driven.
scenarios.hint: What turns HR's 'new hire' signal into automatic provisioning?

scenarios.title: The lingering ex-employee
scenarios.situation: An audit finds 40 departed employees still have active accounts and app access months after leaving.
scenarios.prompt: What prevents this going forward?
evidence: Review the relevant user-group-lifecycle documentation.
choices: Leaver lifecycle workflows — disable accounts, remove licenses/groups, revoke sessions on the HR termination signal
Trusting managers to file tickets
Annual manual reviews
Disabling MFA
scenarios.why: Leaver workflows automate deprovisioning at termination: disable sign-in, revoke refresh tokens (killing active sessions), remove group/license assignments. Lingering access is the #1 identity hygiene failure — automation is the fix, not reminders.
scenarios.hint: What kills accounts, sessions, and access the moment HR records a departure?

scenarios.title: The SaaS sprawl
scenarios.situation: HR creates users in Entra, but each of 30 SaaS apps needs separate manual account creation.
scenarios.prompt: What automates SaaS provisioning?
evidence: Review the relevant user-group-lifecycle documentation.
choices: SCIM-based automatic provisioning — Entra provisions/deprovisions users in SCIM-enabled apps from group membership
CSV uploads per app
Shared credentials per app
One password for all apps
scenarios.why: Entra's provisioning service speaks SCIM to supported apps: assign a group to the app, and users are created/updated/deprovisioned automatically. Group membership becomes the single control point for SaaS access.
scenarios.hint: Which protocol lets Entra push user lifecycle into SaaS apps?

scenarios.title: The contractor request
scenarios.situation: Contractors email IT for access to five different resources; approvals wander between managers for weeks.
scenarios.prompt: What packages this into a self-service flow?
evidence: Review the relevant user-group-lifecycle documentation.
choices: Entitlement management access packages — bundled resources with policy, approval workflow, and automatic expiry
More email threads
A shared contractor account
Permanent access for all
scenarios.why: Access packages bundle the resources a role needs (groups, apps, SharePoint) with request policies: who can request, who approves, and automatic expiration. Self-service requesting with governed approval replaces email chaos.
scenarios.hint: What bundles resources + approvals + expiry into one requestable package?

scenarios.title: The attribute typo
scenarios.situation: A dynamic group rule user.department -eq 'Sales ' (trailing space) silently excludes half the sales team.
scenarios.prompt: What is the lesson for dynamic group design?
evidence: Review the relevant user-group-lifecycle documentation.
choices: Validate rules and monitor membership — attribute hygiene and rule testing prevent silent exclusion; use 'what-if'/preview
Dynamic groups always work perfectly
Manual groups are better
Deleting the group
scenarios.why: Dynamic membership is only as good as attribute data and rule syntax — silent mismatches (trailing spaces, case, null attributes) exclude people without errors. Preview membership, monitor counts, and keep HR attributes clean.
scenarios.hint: The rule ran with no error but excluded people. What practice catches this?

scenarios.title: The delegated help desk

Global Administrator for the help desk
No roles at all
A separate tenant per office

scenarios.hint: What partitions the directory so admin roles apply to one office only?

scenarios.title: User & Group Lifecycle: Design Decision
scenarios.situation: You need to make an architecture/design decision for User & Group Lifecycle in a Sc 300 environment. Multiple approaches are viable, but each has tradeoffs.

Choose the most familiar approach — comfort matters more than fit.
Choose the newest technology — latest is always best.
Delay the decision — more analysis is always better.

scenarios.title: The auth method choice
scenarios.situation: A company with Entra Connect must choose: password hash sync, pass-through, or federation for sign-in.
scenarios.prompt: What is the key trade-off?
evidence: Review the relevant authentication documentation.
choices: PHS: cloud auth, leaked-credential detection, simplest; PTA: on-prem validation, needs high-availability agents; Federation: most control, most complexity
They are identical
Federation is always required
PHS sends plaintext passwords
scenarios.why: PHS syncs password hashes (with leaked-credential detection) and authenticates in the cloud — simplest and most resilient. PTA validates against on-premises AD via agents (needs agent HA). Federation (AD FS) offers deepest control at the highest complexity. Most orgs should prefer PHS + seamless SSO.
scenarios.hint: Cloud-validated, on-prem-validated, or federated — what distinguishes them?

scenarios.title: The double login
scenarios.situation: On the corporate network, users sign into Entra apps but still get prompted for credentials despite being logged into Windows.
scenarios.prompt: What provides silent sign-in on-domain?
evidence: Review the relevant authentication documentation.
choices: Seamless SSO — Kerberos-based silent authentication for domain-joined machines on the corporate network
Disabling passwords
A VPN
Faster typing
scenarios.why: Seamless SSO lets domain-joined machines on the corporate network sign into Entra silently via Kerberos — no password prompt. It's the 'log into Windows, access cloud apps' experience, complementary to PHS/PTA.
scenarios.hint: Domain-joined on the LAN, no password prompt — which feature?

scenarios.title: The SIM-swap victim
scenarios.situation: An executive's phone number was SIM-swapped and the attacker intercepted SMS MFA codes.
scenarios.prompt: What authentication hardening prevents this class of attack?
evidence: Review the relevant authentication documentation.
choices: Phishing-resistant MFA — FIDO2 security keys or Windows Hello for Business / certificate-based auth instead of SMS
Longer SMS codes
SMS to two phones
Security questions
scenarios.why: SMS is the weakest MFA (SIM swap, interception); authenticator push is better; FIDO2/WebAuthn and WHfB are phishing-resistant (bound to origin, no shared secret to intercept). High-value targets need the strong end of the spectrum.
scenarios.hint: Which MFA methods can't be intercepted via SIM swap?

scenarios.title: The first-day login
scenarios.situation: New hires need initial credentials, but emailed passwords keep getting phished or lost.
scenarios.prompt: What is the secure onboarding credential?
evidence: Review the relevant authentication documentation.
choices: Temporary Access Pass — time-limited, single-use passcode for first sign-in and MFA registration
The same default password for everyone
No credentials; accounts active immediately
A sticky note
scenarios.why: Temporary Access Passes give new hires a short-lived passcode to sign in and register strong MFA — no emailed permanent passwords to phish. Scoped lifetime (hours/days) and one-time use by default.
scenarios.hint: What time-limited credential bootstraps a new hire's strong auth?

scenarios.title: The legacy protocol
scenarios.situation: Sign-in logs show attackers using IMAP/SMTP basic auth to password-spray mailboxes, bypassing MFA.
scenarios.prompt: What blocks legacy authentication?
evidence: sign-in log
clientApp: IMAP4 | status: Success | MFA: not applied | 400 attempts from 1 IP
choices: A Conditional Access policy blocking legacy authentication protocols — basic auth can't do MFA
Longer passwords
Disabling the mailboxes
An email to attackers
scenarios.why: Legacy protocols (IMAP, POP, SMTP basic auth) can't enforce MFA — they're the classic MFA-bypass path. The standard control is a CA policy blocking legacy auth (Microsoft now disables basic auth broadly), forcing modern auth everywhere.
scenarios.hint: Basic auth bypasses MFA. What policy kills the bypass?

scenarios.title: The passwordless push
scenarios.situation: The CISO wants to eliminate passwords for office staff entirely.
scenarios.prompt: What are the enterprise passwordless options?
evidence: Review the relevant authentication documentation.
choices: Windows Hello for Business, FIDO2 security keys, or Microsoft Authenticator phone sign-in
Longer passwords
Password expiry every 30 days
Sticky notes with complex passwords
scenarios.why: Entra supports true passwordless: WHfB (device-bound biometrics/PIN), FIDO2 keys (phishing-resistant roaming), and Authenticator phone sign-in. Each removes the phishable shared secret — the password — from the flow.
scenarios.hint: Which three methods let users sign in with no password at all?

scenarios.title: Authentication: Production Incident
scenarios.situation: A production Authentication system is experiencing degraded performance. Users are affected. You need to diagnose and resolve quickly without making things worse.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct incident response sequence for this Authentication degradation?
choices: Assess impact and declare incident severity, check recent changes (deployments, config changes), review key metrics to isolate the layer, implement the least-risky mitigation first, verify recovery, then conduct a blameless post-mortem.
Immediately restart all Authentication components — fastest way to resolve.
Roll back the last deployment without investigation — it's always the deployment.
Wait and monitor — it might resolve itself.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Incident response follows: (1) Assess impact (how bad? who's affected?), (2) Check recent changes (what changed?), (3) Isolate via metrics (which layer?), (4) Mitigate with least risk (don't make it worse), (5) Verify recovery, (6) Post-mortem (prevent recurrence). Skipping steps in Authentication incidents causes extended outages.
scenarios.hint: Remember the incident response phases from the lessons. What's the order?

scenarios.title: The CA rollout
scenarios.situation: An admin creates a 'require MFA for all users' policy and enables it directly — then gets locked out along with the CEO.
scenarios.prompt: What rollout discipline was skipped?
evidence: Review the relevant conditional-access documentation.
choices: Report-only mode + staged rollout + emergency access (break-glass) accounts excluded from CA
Policies don't need testing
Break-glass accounts should be deleted
MFA for everyone is wrong
scenarios.why: CA changes go: report-only (measure impact without enforcing) → pilot → enforce, always excluding emergency-access break-glass accounts. Enabling untested tenant-wide policies is how admins lock themselves out.
scenarios.hint: What mode measures impact without enforcing, and which accounts must always be excluded?

scenarios.title: The compliant device
scenarios.situation: The policy should require MFA only when the device is unmanaged or the location is unfamiliar — managed office devices should sign in smoothly.
scenarios.prompt: Which CA signals enable this?
evidence: Review the relevant conditional-access documentation.
choices: Device compliance (Intune) + network location (named locations) as conditions with appropriate grants
User risk only
The time of day
The user's manager
scenarios.why: CA conditions combine signals — device state (hybrid-joined/compliant via Intune), named locations, client apps, risk — and grants (require MFA, require compliant device, block) apply when conditions match. Precision beats blanket policies.
scenarios.hint: Which two signals distinguish 'managed office device' from everything else?

scenarios.title: The excluded guest
scenarios.situation: A CA policy targets 'All users' but guests keep bypassing MFA requirements.
scenarios.prompt: What is the likely misconfiguration?
evidence: Review the relevant conditional-access documentation.
choices: Guest/external user exclusions or 'all guest users' not included in scope — verify the Users assignment includes guests
Guests are exempt from CA by design
MFA doesn't work for guests
Policies don't apply to B2B
scenarios.why: CA applies to guests when they're in scope — but policies often exclude them accidentally (or target only 'members'). Cross-tenant access settings plus CA for external users need explicit design; 'All users' includes guests unless excluded.
scenarios.hint: Do CA policies cover guests, and where would they be excluded?

scenarios.title: The office IP change
scenarios.situation: The company changes ISPs; the office's public IP changes and suddenly everyone is prompted for MFA as 'unfamiliar location'.
scenarios.prompt: What must be maintained?
evidence: Review the relevant conditional-access documentation.
choices: Named locations — keep the trusted IP ranges current; stale definitions cause false unfamiliar-location signals
Nothing; CA adapts automatically
Deleting the location condition
Disabling MFA
scenarios.why: Named locations encode your trusted networks; when egress IPs change (new ISP, new VPN concentrator), the definitions go stale and location-based policies misfire. IP hygiene is CA hygiene.
scenarios.hint: Egress IPs changed. Which CA definition went stale?

scenarios.title: The sensitive app
scenarios.situation: The finance app needs phishing-resistant MFA always, while the intranet needs only single-factor on managed devices.
scenarios.prompt: How is this expressed?
evidence: Review the relevant conditional-access documentation.
choices: Per-app (target resources) CA policies — different grants for different cloud apps
One policy for everything
No policies for the intranet
Blocking the finance app
scenarios.why: CA's 'target resources' selector lets policies apply per app: strict grants (require authentication strength = phishing-resistant MFA) for finance, lighter for the intranet. Granular policy beats one-size-fits-all.
scenarios.hint: How do different apps get different auth requirements?

scenarios.title: The grant precision
scenarios.situation: The CISO wants 'MFA' to mean specifically phishing-resistant methods for admins, not just any MFA.
scenarios.prompt: What CA grant enforces this?
evidence: Review the relevant conditional-access documentation.
choices: Authentication strengths — require 'phishing-resistant MFA' strength instead of generic 'require MFA'
A longer password policy
An email reminder
Blocking admins
scenarios.why: Authentication strengths let CA demand a specific MFA caliber (e.g., phishing-resistant MFA: FIDO2/WHfB/certificate) rather than any MFA. Generic 'require MFA' still permits SMS — precision matters for privileged users.
scenarios.hint: How do you require FIDO2-grade MFA specifically, not just any MFA?

scenarios.title: Conditional Access: Code Review Finding
scenarios.situation: During code review, you notice a Conditional Access implementation that works but has potential issues. The author is a junior developer who is eager to merge.
scenarios.prompt: How do you handle this Conditional Access code review as a senior team member?
choices: Provide specific, actionable feedback: explain the issue, why it matters, suggest a concrete fix, and offer to pair on the solution. Approve the approach but request changes on the implementation.
Approve immediately — it works, and you don't want to discourage the junior.
Reject outright with 'this is wrong' — they'll figure it out.
Rewrite the code yourself — faster than explaining.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Effective code review for Conditional Access: (1) Be specific about the issue (not 'this is bad'), (2) Explain the impact (why it matters), (3) Suggest a fix (don't just criticize), (4) Offer help (mentorship). This builds both better Conditional Access code and better engineers.
scenarios.hint: Think about the goal of code review — it's not just gatekeeping, it's team growth.
evidence: Review Conditional Access requirements and constraints.

scenarios.title: The midnight change
scenarios.situation: An on-call engineer needs Global Admin for an outage but holds only an eligible assignment.
scenarios.prompt: What is the activation flow?
evidence: Review the relevant pim-access-reviews documentation.
choices: PIM activation — MFA, justification, ticket number, time-bound (e.g., 4 hours), then automatic deactivation
Email the CEO
Permanent assignment
Shared admin password
scenarios.why: Eligible assignments activate just-in-time: the engineer requests, completes MFA, gives justification, gets the role for a bounded window, and it expires automatically. Every activation is logged for audit.
scenarios.hint: Eligible but not active — what turns it on for the outage window?

scenarios.title: The sensitive role
scenarios.situation: Activations of Privileged Authentication Administrator should require a second person's approval.
scenarios.prompt: What PIM control adds this?
evidence: Review the relevant pim-access-reviews documentation.
choices: Approval workflow on the role's PIM settings — designated approvers must approve before activation
An email notification only
No control possible
Deleting the role
scenarios.why: PIM role settings support approval workflows: activation requests route to approvers with justification. The most sensitive roles get approvers; routine ones may allow self-approval with MFA — tiered by risk.
scenarios.hint: Which PIM setting puts a human gate before activation?

scenarios.title: The stale access
scenarios.situation: Guest accounts from a 2022 project still have Teams and SharePoint access; nobody remembers approving them.
scenarios.prompt: What recurring control catches this?
evidence: Review the relevant pim-access-reviews documentation.
choices: Access reviews — periodic reviewer attestation of guests' continued need, auto-removing denied/ignored access
A one-time cleanup
Trusting project memory
More guests
scenarios.why: Access reviews ask designated reviewers (managers, group owners) to certify continued access; denied or unreviewed access is removed automatically. They're the recurring hygiene for guests, access packages, and role assignments.
scenarios.hint: What periodically asks 'does this person still need access?'

scenarios.title: The rogue assignment
scenarios.situation: Someone grants a user permanent Global Admin outside PIM; nobody notices for weeks.
scenarios.prompt: What detects privileged role drift?
evidence: Review the relevant pim-access-reviews documentation.
choices: PIM alerts + access reviews on role assignments — alert on permanent assignments and out-of-policy grants
Manual portal checks yearly
Trust
Deleting PIM
scenarios.why: PIM's security alerts flag risky assignments (permanent privileged roles, assignments outside PIM); pairing with recurring access reviews on the roles themselves catches drift. Permanent privileged assignment is the finding, not the norm.
scenarios.hint: What notices a permanent Global Admin grant that bypassed PIM?

scenarios.title: The never-ending contractor
scenarios.situation: Contractor access packages were approved 'for the project' but never expire; contractors from 2023 still have access.
scenarios.prompt: What enforces an end date?
evidence: Review the relevant pim-access-reviews documentation.
choices: Access package assignment policies with expiration + recurring access reviews — time-bound access by design
Permanent assignments
A calendar reminder
Hope
scenarios.why: Entitlement management bakes in lifetimes: assignment policies set durations, and access reviews re-certify. 'For the project' must translate to a date — otherwise every temporary grant becomes permanent.
scenarios.hint: How do you make 'temporary access' actually temporary?

scenarios.title: The standing VM admin
scenarios.situation: Admins hold permanent local admin on 200 Azure VMs.
scenarios.prompt: What reduces this standing privilege?
evidence: Review the relevant pim-access-reviews documentation.

More local admins
Shared local passwords
Disabling RDP
scenarios.why: JIT VM access opens management ports only for approved, time-bound windows with MFA; combined with PIM for the Azure roles, standing admin evaporates. Permanent local admin on fleets is the legacy pattern.
scenarios.hint: What replaces always-on admin ports with approved time windows?

scenarios.title: The legacy app
scenarios.situation: A 15-year-old internal app supports SAML but not modern OAuth2/OIDC.
scenarios.prompt: How does Entra single sign-on work for it?
evidence: Review the relevant app-integration documentation.
choices: Entra SAML SSO from the app gallery (or custom SAML app) — Entra acts as the IdP via SAML assertions
It can't integrate
Shared passwords
A VPN
scenarios.why: Entra supports SAML 2.0 apps: it becomes the identity provider, issuing SAML assertions the app trusts. The gallery has thousands of pre-integrated apps; custom SAML covers the rest. Legacy protocol support doesn't mean legacy passwords.
scenarios.hint: The app speaks SAML only. How does Entra SSO it?

scenarios.title: The modern app
scenarios.situation: A new internal SPA needs sign-in with tokens for API calls.
scenarios.prompt: Which protocol and library fit?
evidence: Review the relevant app-integration documentation.
choices: OpenID Connect with MSAL — standardized auth code flow with PKCE, token acquisition and caching handled
SAML for the SPA
Basic auth headers
Cookies with passwords
scenarios.why: OIDC (built on OAuth2) is the modern app protocol; MSAL implements it correctly (auth code + PKCE, token cache, silent renewal). SPAs must never use implicit flow or handle passwords — the library enforces the safe patterns.
scenarios.hint: Modern SPA needing tokens — which protocol and library?

scenarios.title: The overreaching app
scenarios.situation: A simple time-tracking app requests 'Read all mail' permissions; users are consenting blindly.
scenarios.prompt: What admin controls prevent excessive consent?
evidence: Review the relevant app-integration documentation.
choices: Consent policies + admin consent workflow — restrict which permissions users can consent to; risky permissions need admin approval
Letting users consent to anything
Deleting the app
Ignoring it
scenarios.why: Admin consent workflows and consent policies gate which app permissions users can grant themselves; high-privilege permissions (like Mail.Read) require admin approval. Blind consent is how overreaching apps get enterprise data.
scenarios.hint: Who approves an app asking for 'read all mail'?

scenarios.title: The on-prem app
scenarios.situation: An on-premises intranet app (IIS, Windows auth) must be reachable by remote users without a VPN, with Entra pre-authentication.
scenarios.prompt: What publishes it securely?
evidence: Review the relevant app-integration documentation.
choices: Entra Application Proxy — cloud pre-auth + connector-driven private access, no inbound firewall holes
A public IP on the IIS server
VPN for everyone
Exposing Windows auth to the internet
scenarios.why: Application Proxy's lightweight connectors make outbound connections; Entra pre-authenticates users in the cloud, then the connector delivers traffic to the internal app. No DMZ, no inbound ports, modern auth for legacy apps.
scenarios.hint: How do remote users reach an on-prem app with no VPN and no inbound ports?

scenarios.title: The app ownership
scenarios.situation: Nobody knows who owns the 300 enterprise apps in the tenant; orphaned apps accumulate permissions.
scenarios.prompt: What governance applies?
evidence: Review the relevant app-integration documentation.
choices: App owners assigned + access reviews on app role assignments + periodic app inventory hygiene
Deleting random apps
Ignoring ownership
More apps
scenarios.why: Enterprise apps need owners (accountable humans), reviewed role assignments, and lifecycle hygiene — orphaned apps with broad permissions are a standing attack surface. Governance treats apps like identities: provisioned, reviewed, deprovisioned.
scenarios.hint: Who is accountable for each enterprise app's permissions?

scenarios.title: The stolen token

Longer token lifetimes
No protection possible
Disabling the app

scenarios.title: The spray pattern
scenarios.situation: The SOC sees thousands of failed logins across hundreds of accounts from a few IPs.
scenarios.prompt: Where is this investigated, and what is it?
evidence: sign-in log sample
result: 50126 (bad password) | 4,200 events | 380 users | 3 source IPs | 1 success ← investigate
choices: Sign-in logs in Entra — password spray pattern; investigate via KQL, then block IPs / enforce MFA / check for successes
The firewall logs only
The application logs
Nowhere — it's normal

scenarios.title: The mystery role grant

scenarios.prompt: Where is the authoritative record?
evidence: Review the relevant monitoring documentation.
choices: Entra audit logs — every directory change (who, what, when) is logged; filter for role assignment events
The user's word
The activity log of Azure resources
Guessing

evidence: Review Identity Protection requirements and constraints.

scenarios.title: Identity Protection: Production Incident
scenarios.situation: A production Identity Protection system is experiencing degraded performance. Users are affected. You need to diagnose and resolve quickly without making things worse.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct incident response sequence for this Identity Protection degradation?
choices: Assess impact and declare incident severity, check recent changes (deployments, config changes), review key metrics to isolate the layer, implement the least-risky mitigation first, verify recovery, then conduct a blameless post-mortem.
Immediately restart all Identity Protection components — fastest way to resolve.
Roll back the last deployment without investigation — it's always the deployment.
Wait and monitor — it might resolve itself.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Incident response follows: (1) Assess impact (how bad? who's affected?), (2) Check recent changes (what changed?), (3) Isolate via metrics (which layer?), (4) Mitigate with least risk (don't make it worse), (5) Verify recovery, (6) Post-mortem (prevent recurrence). Skipping steps in Identity Protection incidents causes extended outages.
scenarios.hint: Remember the incident response phases from the lessons. What's the order?
evidence: Review Identity Protection requirements and constraints.

lessons.title: Authentication — Core concepts
concepts: Hybrid auth: legacy protocols (IMAP, POP, SMTP basic auth) can't enforce MFA — they're the classic MFA-bypass path.
PHS vs PTA vs federation: most orgs should prefer PHS + seamless SSO.
Seamless SSO lets domain-joined machines on the corporate network sign into Entra silently via Kerberos — no password prompt.
Silent auth: the standard control is a CA policy blocking legacy auth (Microsoft now disables basic auth broadly), forcing modern auth everywhere.

MFA strength: temporary Access Passes give new hires a short-lived passcode to sign in and register strong MFA — no emailed permanent passwords to phish. SMS is the weakest MFA (SIM swap, interception); authenticator push is better; FIDO2/WebAuthn and WHfB are phishing-resistant (bound to origin, no shared secret to intercept).

lessons.title: Monitoring — Core concepts
concepts: Sign-in logs are the identity investigation surface: filter failures by IP, look for any success amid the spray (compromise!), then respond — block, force password reset, require MFA. Sign-in logs show authentication; audit logs show administration.

Password spray: identity Protection ingests breach corpuses and matches them to your users (via PHS hash comparison) — user-risk policies then force password change. The full loop: risk policy contains (force password change at high user risk), and risk detections stream to Sentinel/SOAR for ticketing and investigation.

Audit logs record all Entra control-plane changes with actor, target, and timestamp — the non-repudiable record for 'who granted what'. Workbooks query the streamed Entra logs (sign-in, audit, risk) into living dashboards — MFA registration gaps, risk trends, stale access — the identity posture view leadership actually needs.
Identity hygiene is measured, not assumed.

lessons.title: Identity and Access (Entra ID) — Core concepts
concepts: Entra ID is the identity plane: tenants hold users, groups, and app registrations; Conditional Access policies evaluate signals (who, what device, where, what risk) and enforce grant controls (MFA, compliant device, block).
PIM makes privilege just-in-time: assignments are eligible (can activate) rather than active (standing), with MFA-gated activation, approval, justification, and automatic expiry.

Identity Protection turns risk detections (unfamiliar locations, leaked credentials, anomalous tokens) into policy: require MFA at medium risk, block or force password change at high risk — notify-only is not protection.
Emergency-access (break-glass) accounts are excluded from Conditional Access by design, monitored with sign-in alerts, and kept offline — they are the recovery path when policy itself fails.
Access reviews sustain least privilege: resource owners periodically attest guest and privileged access, with auto-removal for non-response, so grants decay instead of accumulating.

Legacy authentication (basic auth, old protocols) cannot do MFA and is a top attack vector: block it for users, and handle the rare immovable service account as a narrow, monitored, time-boxed exception.

Common trap: writing a CA policy with broad targets and silent exclusions/conditions, then wondering why it never fires — diagnose with What If and sign-in logs.
Common trap: treating a legacy-auth exception as permanent instead of a scoped, monitored, dated migration.

lessons.title: How to Use This Microsoft Identity and Access Administrator Bootcamp
concepts: The study order is deliberate — follow it: Start Here (this domain: course overview, study strategy, key terminology) → Lessons (the deep-dives, in domain order) → Drills (practice scenarios, untimed, with full explanations) → Labs (hands-on exercises) → Mock Assessment (timed simulation). Each layer assumes the one before. Skipping straight to the mock burns your one realistic practice run.

What 'identity administrator' means in practice: this bootcamp prepares you for the real-world responsibilities of a identity administrator, not just exam questions. Every lesson connects theory to the decisions you'll make on the job — what to check first, what to try next, how to explain your reasoning.

The SC-300 Microsoft Identity and Access Administrator exam strategy: (a) first pass — read every lesson in order without skipping, taking notes on concepts that feel unfamiliar; (b) second pass — work every scenario and lab, reading the 'why' explanations even for correct answers; (c) final pass — take the timed mock under realistic conditions (no pauses, no references).

How to read the scenarios: every scenario has a 'why' explanation — read it even when you got the answer right, because it explains the WRONG answers too (and real exams design wrong answers from those same misconceptions). The hint is there to unblock you, not to give away the answer.

Active recall beats re-reading: after each lesson, close the page and explain the key concepts out loud in your own words. If you can't explain it simply, you don't understand it yet — re-read that section.
Spaced repetition: revisit completed domains after 2-3 days. The bootcamp tracks your progress — use the dashboard to identify weak areas and drill those specifically before the mock.

example.code:
Week 1: Start Here + first 3 domains (lessons only)
Week 2: Remaining domains (lessons + scenarios)
Week 3: All labs + weak-area review
Week 4: Timed mock → review misses → targeted re-study
Exam/Interview: Confident and prepared
example.walkthrough: This 4-week plan assumes 1-2 hours per day. Adjust the pace to your schedule, but keep the order: lessons before scenarios, scenarios before labs, everything before the mock. The mock is a diagnostic tool — take it when you're ready to find gaps, not when you're still learning fundamentals.

pitfalls: Skipping the Start Here domain because 'I already know the basics' — the study strategy and terminology sections prevent wasted effort later.
Doing scenarios before reading the lessons — you'll memorize answers without understanding the concepts, and the mock will expose it.
Ignoring the 'why' explanations for correct answers — the wrong-answer analysis is where deep understanding comes from.
Taking the mock too early as a 'practice test' — it's a final validation, not a study tool. Use it once when ready.

lessons.title: Microsoft Identity and Access Administrator: Field Overview and Key Terminology
concepts: Microsoft Identity and Access Administrator sits at the intersection of theory and hands-on practice. The professionals who excel are those who can both explain the 'why' and execute the 'how' under pressure.

Key terminology is the price of admission — every domain in this bootcamp assumes you can use the core vocabulary precisely. When you encounter an unfamiliar term, stop and learn it before continuing.
The field rewards systems thinkers: people who see how components connect, not just isolated facts. The Systems Anatomy domain teaches this explicitly — start there after finishing Start Here.
Documentation is a professional skill, not an afterthought. As you learn, practice explaining concepts as if writing a runbook — clear, sequential, with the 'why' for each step.

Weak answer: 'I know about X.'
Strong answer: 'X works by [mechanism]. In practice, I've used it to [application]. The key consideration is [tradeoff].'

pitfalls: Using jargon without understanding — interviewers will probe deeper, and vague terminology collapses under follow-up questions.
Learning tools before concepts — tools change, but the underlying principles persist across versions and vendors.

lessons.title: Study Strategy: From Learning to Mastery
concepts: The learning pyramid: reading alone retains ~10%, but teaching someone else retains ~90%. After each domain, explain the concepts to an imaginary colleague — or better, a real one.
Deliberate practice: don't just re-read weak areas, actively test yourself on them. The scenario drills are designed for this — they force retrieval, not recognition.
Error analysis: every wrong answer is data. Log your misses by domain and concept. Patterns in your errors reveal exactly where to focus.
The 80/20 rule: 80% of exam/interview questions come from 20% of the material — the core concepts that everything else builds on. This bootcamp front-loads those in the early domains.
Sleep consolidates learning: study sessions followed by sleep outperform cramming. Don't sacrifice rest for extra hours — your brain needs downtime to build connections.

example.code:
Study session template (60 min):
  0-10:  Review previous session's key concepts (retrieval)
  10-40: New lesson + scenario practice (learning)
  40-50: Lab exercise (application)
  50-60: Write summary notes (consolidation)

End each session by writing tomorrow's starting point.
example.walkthrough: This template prevents the two biggest study failures: passive re-reading (no retrieval) and marathon sessions (diminishing returns). The 10-minute review at the start compounds over weeks — by exam day, early material is rock solid.

lessons.title: What Success Looks Like: Exam and Interview Readiness

The night before: no new material. Review your error log, skim key concept summaries, and rest. Confidence comes from preparation, not last-minute cramming.

lessons.title: Capstone Project: Build Your Microsoft Identity and Access Administrator Portfolio Piece

Scope ruthlessly: a small project done well beats an ambitious project done poorly. Pick something you can complete in 2-4 weekends.

lessons.title: Presenting Your Work: From Build to Interview Story
concepts: The STAR method for technical stories: Situation (context) → Task (your responsibility) → Action (what you did, specifically) → Result (measurable outcome).
Lead with the problem, not the technology. 'We needed to automate X because manual process took Y hours' is more compelling than 'I used tool Z.'
Quantify everything: time saved, errors reduced, performance improved, users served. Numbers make stories credible and memorable.
Prepare for deep dives: interviewers will pick one detail and probe. Know your architecture cold — every component, every tradeoff, every alternative you considered.
Show the messy parts: what went wrong, how you debugged it, what you'd do differently. This demonstrates maturity more than a flawless narrative.

example.code:
Weak: 'I built a thing with React.'
Strong: 'Our team spent 6 hours weekly on manual deployments. I built an automated pipeline using [tools] that cut deployment time to 15 minutes and eliminated config drift. The hardest part was [challenge] — I solved it by [approach].'
example.walkthrough: Notice the structure: problem (6 hours wasted) → action (built pipeline) → result (15 min, no drift) → depth (hardest part + solution). Practice telling your capstone story in 2 minutes, then be ready to go deep on any part.

pitfalls: Vague claims without specifics — 'I improved performance' means nothing; 'I reduced load time from 4s to 800ms by...' is compelling.
Only preparing the happy path — interviewers specifically ask about failures and challenges.
Memorizing a script — stories should feel conversational, not rehearsed. Know the beats, not the words.
No demo ready — always have a live demo, screenshots, or video. 'Let me show you' beats 'trust me.'

lessons.title: Risk Policies
concepts: Identity Protection detects risky sign-ins and risky users using ML on trillions of signals
Risk levels: low, medium, high — based on unfamiliar locations, anonymous IPs, malware-linked IPs, etc.
Policies: require MFA for medium+ risk, block or require password change for high risk
Risk must be remediated — dismissed risks don't improve the user's risk state

example.code:
Risk policy configuration:
  Sign-in risk policy:
    - High risk: Block access
    - Medium risk: Require MFA
  User risk policy:
    - High risk: Require password change
    
  Apply to: All users (start with report-only, then enforce)
example.walkthrough: Start in report-only mode to measure impact. Enforcing without testing locks out legitimate users.

pitfalls: Enforcing without report-only testing — legitimate users get blocked
Ignoring risk remediation — dismissed risks stay; remediate to clear
No exclusions for break-glass — ensure emergency access accounts bypass policies
lessons.try_it: Configure risk policies in report-only mode. Analyze the impact report before enforcing.

lessons.title: Access Reviews
concepts: Access reviews ensure users still need their access — combat privilege creep
Review types: groups, roles, access packages — schedule recurring reviews
Reviewers: managers, group owners, or self-review — choose based on context
Auto-apply: remove denied access automatically — don't rely on manual follow-up

example.code:
Guest access review:
  Scope: All guest users in Teams groups
  Reviewers: Group owners
  Frequency: Quarterly
  Action: Auto-remove denied guests after 30 days
  
  Result: 40% of guests removed (stale access eliminated)
example.walkthrough: Guest accounts are a major risk — they accumulate and are rarely reviewed. Automated reviews solve this.

pitfalls: One-time reviews — access creep returns; schedule recurring
No auto-apply — denied access that isn't removed is still a risk
Wrong reviewers — managers who don't know what access means can't review effectively
lessons.try_it: Create an access review for privileged roles. Configure auto-apply and verify denied access is removed.

lessons.title: Eligible Assignments
concepts: PIM converts standing admin access to eligible — users activate only when needed
Activation requires: MFA, approval, justification, time limit (max 8 hours)
Reduces attack surface: compromised accounts don't have persistent admin rights
Audit trail: every activation is logged with who, why, and what they did

example.code:
PIM configuration:
  Role: Global Administrator
  Assignment: Eligible (not Active)
  Activation: MFA + approval + 4-hour max + justification
  Alert: Notify security team on activation
  
  Result: 0 standing global admins (was: 5)
example.walkthrough: Zero standing admins is the goal. Every activation is a conscious, logged, time-limited decision.

pitfalls: Standing admin assignments — defeats the purpose; make everything eligible
No approval workflow — self-approval is better than nothing, but manager approval is stronger
Long activation durations — 8 hours max; shorter is better
lessons.try_it: Convert a standing admin role to PIM eligible. Configure activation requirements and test the workflow.

lessons.title: Policy Design Patterns
concepts: Start with baseline policies: require MFA for admins, require compliant devices, block legacy auth
Use report-only mode to measure impact before enforcing
Layer policies: each policy is an AND within, OR across — design accordingly
Test with What If tool — simulate before deploying

example.code:
Policy layers:
  1. Block: Legacy authentication (all users)
  2. Require: MFA for admins (all cloud apps)
  3. Require: Compliant device for sensitive apps
  4. Block: High-risk sign-ins (all users)
  
  Order doesn't matter — all policies evaluate; most restrictive wins.
example.walkthrough: Legacy auth bypasses MFA — blocking it is the single highest-impact CA policy.

pitfalls: Enforcing without testing — What If tool exists for a reason
Too many overlapping policies — simplifies to confusion; consolidate where possible
No break-glass exclusions — lock yourself out and you'll regret it
lessons.try_it: Design a CA policy set for your organization. Test each in report-only, then enforce in phases.

lessons.title: B2B Collaboration
concepts: B2B lets external users access your resources with their own credentials — no password sharing
Invitation process: invite → redeem → access — track each stage

Cross-tenant access settings control trust between organizations

  1. Create access package: 'Partner - Project Alpha'

     - Approval: Project manager

  3. Auto-provisioned on approval, auto-removed on expiration

simulations.title: Write the Conditional Access policy
simulations.brief: The CISO wants: admins always do MFA, legacy auth blocked everywhere, break-glass excluded. Build the policy logic.

steps.text: First: which users does the admin-MFA policy target?

choices.label: All users — simplest
choices.feedback: Blanket MFA on all users on day one creates helpdesk chaos. Start with the highest-risk population.

choices.label: Directory roles (admins) — highest privilege first
choices.feedback: Correct — admins are the highest-value targets; require MFA there first.

steps.text: The helpdesk is drowning in MFA lockouts from the rollout. Reconsider:

choices.label: Target directory roles first, phase the rest
choices.feedback: Right — phased rollout by risk, not big-bang.

steps.text: The break-glass accounts: include them in the MFA policy?

choices.label: Yes — no exceptions
choices.feedback: If MFA breaks, the break-glass accounts are your only way back in. Excluding them (with monitoring) is the standard.

choices.label: No — exclude them, but alert on any use
choices.feedback: Correct — break-glass stays excluded from CA but every use pages the SOC.

simulations.debrief: You built the CA logic like an identity admin: admins first, phased rollout, break-glass excluded but monitored.

simulations.title: The CA policy with a hole
simulations.brief: This Conditional Access policy looks complete. Click the lines that leave a hole attackers drive through.

steps.config:
CA policy: admin-baseline
1. Users: all directory roles
2. Cloud apps: all
3. Conditions: none
4. Grant: require MFA
5. Session: none
6. Enabled: report-only

issues.description: No conditions means the policy cannot scope by risk, location, or device — it is all-or-nothing.
issues.fix: Add conditions (e.g. risky sign-ins, non-compliant devices) so the policy adapts to context.

issues.description: Report-only mode evaluates but never enforces — the policy protects nothing.
issues.fix: After validating in report-only, switch the policy to On.

simulations.debrief: You found the CA holes: no conditions and report-only forever. A policy that never enforces is documentation, not protection.

simulations.title: Joiner-mover-leaver
simulations.brief: Order the identity lifecycle so access follows the person — granted on arrival, adjusted on move, removed on exit.

items: Revoke all access and disable the account
Provision account and baseline access
Adjust group memberships for the new role
HR triggers the joiner event

simulations.debrief: You ordered the lifecycle: trigger, provision, adjust on move, revoke on leave. Orphaned accounts are a joiner-mover-leaver failure.

simulations.title: The MFA outage
simulations.brief: Users report MFA push never arrives. The auth service is healthy. Work it before the helpdesk melts.

steps.symptom: MFA push notifications never arrive; SMS codes work fine.
evidence: az login
Already signed in as candidate@interstitium (simulated — no real auth).
options: Check the push notification service / app registration health — pushes ride a different path than SMS
Reset every user's MFA registration immediately
Disable MFA until the pushes recover
Tell users to keep retrying — pushes are flaky
steps.explain: Push and SMS are different delivery paths — one failing while the other works isolates the fault to the push path (notification hub / app). Mass resets or disabling MFA punish users for a platform issue.

simulations.debrief: You isolated the fault by comparing paths: SMS works, push does not, so the push delivery path is the suspect. Compare, don't guess.
